Hybrid quantum-classical frameworks leverage quantum computing for machine learning; however, variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are limited by local measurements. We introduce an adaptive non-local observable (ANO) paradigm within VQCs for quantum reinforcement learning (QRL), jointly optimizing circuit parameters and multi-qubit measurements. On multiple benchmark tasks, ANOVQC agents outperform baseline VQCs. Ablation studies reveal that adaptive measurements enhance the function space without increasing circuit depth. results.title: Evaluating Parameter-Based Training Performance of Neural Networks and Variational Quantum Circuits
results.content:
Title: Evaluating Parameter-Based Training Performance of Neural Networks and Variational Quantum Circuits
We carry out most VQC experiments on a simulator but approximate real hardware training times by running selected circuits on actual quantum devices. To our knowledge, no existing work thoroughly compares NNs and VQCs for machine learning tasks with a detailed focus on model architectures, parameter counts, and training times. We compare models with varying parameter counts and approximate the time required to train on real quantum hardware. In this work, we compare the training performance of classical NNs to VQCs on selected machine learning tasks. For each task, we evaluate a set of NNs with varying parameter counts and a corresponding set of VQCs that also differ in their parameter counts, aiming to identify one NN and one VQC with comparable performance. We use the same classical training loop for all SL tasks, interchanging NNs or VQCs as the model. For the Iris and Wine datasets, the NN grid search covers {1,2,3} hidden layers ×\times×{3,6,9,12} nodes per layer, producing 12 NNs. For the VQC, we use angle or amplitude embedding and vary the number of variational layers from 1 to 6, also yielding 12 configurations. We consider models with at least 0.96 test accuracy as well-performing, yielding 4 of 12 NNs and 5 of 12 VQCs. Overall, VQCs slightly outperform NNs. We select an NN with 75 parameters (1 hidden layer, 9 nodes) and a VQC with 28 parameters (angle embedding, 2 variational layers). Even in our small-scale tasks, we see a trend of longer training times for larger models, especially for VQCs. This trend may be more pronounced in complex tasks where standard NNs can have millions of parameters, potentially offering a more substantial advantage to VQCs that require fewer parameters [19, 24]. However, the VQCs required substantially longer training durations, with simulator-based training being 26 to 457 times slower than the NNs. By executing a subset of circuits on real quantum hardware, we approximated current hardware training times for the VQCs. Because these tasks used at most five qubits, simulations were relatively fast, resulting in real-hardware training times that were longer than those on the simulator. Future work could assess more complex tasks to deepen our understanding of VQCs’ potential compared to NNs. Furthermore, our real-hardware tests only assessed circuit execution times and not final outputs, leaving device fidelity unexamined.

results.title: AutoML-driven optimization of variational quantum circuit - ScienceDirect
results.content: We optimize both circuit structures and training settings for quantum architecture search. Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) offer a powerful framework for quantum machine learning models, where circuit parameters are optimized to learn specific tasks. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned on a small set of labeled data from a downstream task to develop a performance predictor that estimates the performance of quantum circuits based on their structures and training settings. Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) have become a prominent approach in quantum machine learning [1], where the parameters of quantum circuits are variationally optimized to perform specific tasks. By exploiting quantum entanglement and superposition, VQCs can effectively model complex functions using a relatively small number of parameters, making them applicable to a wide range of tasks, including classification [2], generation [3], optimization [4], quantum neural networks [5], quantum reinforcement learning [6], and quantum chemistry [7]. In the early stage of VQC research, quantum circuit structures are predefined, with optimization focused exclusively on the parameter values. QAS algorithms employ a variety of techniques to optimize both the structures and parameters of quantum circuits [9]. By incorporating these advancements, QAS eliminates the need for the manual design of circuit structures, enabling more efficient quantum circuit optimization and broadening the potential applications of VQCs in practical quantum machine learning tasks. Nevertheless, its ability to automate tasks such as selecting optimal quantum circuit structures, tuning training settings, and other critical components holds great promise for significantly enhancing the efficiency and performance of VQCs. This could open up exciting new possibilities for both research and real-world applications in quantum machine learning. In this work, we present an AutoML-driven approach that automates not only the optimization of VQC structures and parameters, but also extends to the tuning of training settings such as optimizer choice, learning rate, and batch size. Through numerical simulation experiments, we demonstrate the potential of our approach to enhance both the performance and efficiency of VQCs in quantum machine learning applications. Our VQC optimization framework employs a predictor-based approach to estimate the performance of quantum circuit structures and training settings. In this study, we proposed a novel approach for optimizing VQCs by integrating a GCN-based predictor, pretraining, and joint optimization of circuit structures and training settings.
